transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Less than three weeks to go before the midterm elections,
the economy is top of mind among voters.
A Pew Research Center survey conducted this fall
reveals many voters are worried about prices and affordability.
70% of U.S. adults say they've cut back on spending for extras,
such as eating out or streaming services.
54% say they have not been able to save money for the future.
Well, more than 70 million Americans who collect social security
and/or supplemental security income
will see their benefits increase 3.6% next year.
The cost of living adjustment for retirees and disabled recipients
amounts to an extra $75 a month.
Whether the annual adjustment keeps up with inflation is another matter.
New Labor Department report shows inflation is heating up.
A federal judge in California has halted
the Trump administration's controversial reorganization
of the Department of Agriculture.
And Pierce-Kirk Sigler reports this also stops a relocation
of the headquarters of the U.S. Forest Service for now.
The Trump administration has planned to close or consolidate
dozens of federal research stations, primarily in the northwest,
and move the headquarters of the U.S. Forest Service from Washington, D.C. to Utah.
That's ignited particular controversy
due to the fact that Utah has more desert lands than forests
and is on the forefront of an effort by conservative western states
to take over control of federal public lands.
The judge in the case brought by federal employee unions wrote
that this broader reorganization can't be done without the consent
and funding of Congress.
The judge gave the administration two days to respond to most of the order,
but broadly halted the USDA reorganization.
Trump officials have said it's needed to modernize and make the agency more efficient,
while unions and conservationists are likening it to a dismantling.
Kirk Sigler, NPR News.
We're learning more about the circumstances
surrounding Krista Pike's botched execution attempt in Tennessee last month.
Pike was given two rounds of lethal injection drugs, but she survived.
Catherine Sweeney of conversationWPLN reports 911 recordings are offering new details.
No one has ever survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs.
So, Tennessee's execution protocols had no guidance.
Recordings obtained by WPLN depict a communication breakdown
that found dispatchers trying to figure out if requests for help were prank calls.
Prison workers denied needing medical help several times,
even after an ambulance, fire trucks and police escorts were sent out.
Here's a short exchange.
We have responders that are standing by and we're just trying to verify.
I'm being told that nobody from our facility called you.
Pike was eventually taken to a hospital and has since been released back to prison.
For NPR News, I'm Catherine Sweeney in Nashville.
U.S. stocks trading lower at the Nasdaq down more than 580 points.
This is NPR News.
The Trump administration seems to have blocked some intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
Richard Haas, a former adviser during the George W. Bush administration,
says it's all too consistent with the pattern of U.S. foreign policy toward Ukraine's
defense against Russia since President Trump took office.
We have consistently done things for Russia and we have consistently done things to Ukraine.
And that is, this is simply the latest shoe to draw.
Have you ever walked into a mall where a friendly salesperson approaches you
with a free sample of skincare cream?
An NPR investigation has found that what follows can cost customers thousands of dollars.
NPR's Monica Estradaeva has details.
Mark Eckert discovered the charges after his mother's bank account overdrew.
What kind of a spa charges anyone $54,000?
Mary Eckert is one of the hundreds of customers NPR uncovered that had been hit
with thousands of dollars in charges from beauty stores in malls
and purchases that they say they never authorized, didn't want, and cannot return.
The stores are independently owned, but they all sell skincare products
distributed by the Mazal Group.
Based in California, the owner is from Israel.
The federal government was looking into Israeli-owned skincare stores a decade ago
for immigration violations.
NPR found evidence that visa fraud is still happening in those stores today.
Monica Estradaeva, NPR News.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Less than three weeks before midterms, voters worry about prices, affordability, and savings, per Pew survey
Social Security and SSI recipients to get 3.6% cost-of-living increase, about $75 a month
Federal judge in California halts Trump administration's USDA reorganization and Forest Service headquarters move to Utah
Tennessee 911 recordings reveal communication breakdown during Krista Pike's botched execution attempt
Trump administration reportedly blocks some intelligence sharing with Ukraine, according to former Bush adviser Richard Haass
NPR investigation finds mall skincare stores run by Mazal Group racking up thousands in unauthorized charges
